title: Job, a good man (Job 1–2)
hookLine: a good man loses everything, and still does not curse God
carry: the lord gave, the lord took

lines: A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.
cards: "There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." It opens like a folk tale: once upon a time, far away. Nobody knows for sure where Uz was, and the book never says Job was an Israelite.
He's just a man, somewhere east, with seven sons, three daughters, thousands of sheep and camels, and a habit of getting up early to offer sacrifices in case his children had sinned at their parties.
Then, in a single day, four messengers arrive. Raiders took the oxen. Fire fell on the sheep.
Raiders took the camels. And the last: a great wind hit the house where his children were eating, and they are all dead.

teach.b: The King James Bible calls Job "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." Perfect here means whole, blameless, not flawless. First, the reader sees what Job never does: a scene in heaven.
The heavenly beings come before God, and among them is one called, in Hebrew, ha-satan.
The satan, with the word the in front, more a job title than a name: the adversary, the accuser.
Christian tradition has identified him with the devil; some scholars read him here as a member of the heavenly court whose role is to accuse.

teach.h: DOTH JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOUGHT?
teach.b: God points out Job, and the accuser asks the question the whole book turns on: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Is anyone good for free, or only for the reward? Take it all away, and see.

Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."
Then his own body is struck with sores, and he sits in ashes, scraping himself with broken pottery. His wife, who has also just lost ten children, says: curse God, and die.
Job answers: "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?"
The reader knows about the heavenly scene; Job never finds out.

teach.h: THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.
teach.b: He lives through all of it without the explanation.

how: Christians often read the book of Job in times of grief and suffering, and Job's words "the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away" are said at many Christian funerals.

o: a good man from Uz who loses everything in a single day
a prophet who sulked when God spared the city of Nineveh
an Israelite king punished for his many hidden sins

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.

s: the book says Job was an Israelite
it places him in the land of Uz, and never calls him an Israelite.
in Hebrew, the accuser has the word the in front of his name
ha-satan: the adversary, more like a title than a name.
Job curses God after losing everything
he says, "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."

games.q: in one day you've lost your herds, your servants and all ten of your children. what do you do?
o: tear your robe, fall to the ground, and worship.
demand that God explain himself, right now.
games.why: Job grieves with his whole body and still blesses God's name. the demands for an answer come later, and the book keeps those too.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose trouble makes no sense, a sick child, a friend whose life fell apart through no fault of their own, and don't try to explain it; Job's story begins by refusing to.
If you pray, name them before God and leave the why unanswered; if not, wish them strength, like a hand on a shoulder.

wordCard.voice: Job. A good man from the land of Uz who loses everything, and whose book asks whether anyone loves God for nothing.

orig.note: Hebrew: the adversary, the accuser. in Job it carries the word the, like a title.

carryVoice: Your line: the Lord gave, the Lord took. Job says it in the ashes, not after the ending. Go gently.
